program.name: Swift Agent — OSS Direction
program.description: Complete the unbuilt rungs of the adoption ladder: a hosted playground and one-click setup (scaffold CLI + managed-host deploy template), on a repaired local stack, with the three publishable packages and create-swift-agent released to public npm via a manual workflow_dispatch trigger the owner presses once.
program.executionModeReason: Three separately-shippable release surfaces must each be independently green and independently reversible: a container image published to GHCR, npm packaging metadata for three packages, and a publicly-hosted playground deployment. The publishing flip is a genuine expand -> migrate -> contract migration with load-bearing ordering (Apache-2.0 and public publishConfig must be in the tree before any image publishes; the local registry harness must exist before the scaffold CLI can install the packages as real dependencies), and no single agent session can coherently own a new two-part deployable app (apps/playground backend + frontend), a twelve-surface repository posture flip, a scaffold CLI, a container pipeline, and a managed-host deploy template. After the root repair the packaging chain and the hosting chain are causally independent and run in parallel, which is material parallelism rather than cosmetic decomposition.

technology.playgroundHost: Fly.io or Railway (decided in WS-47) — deliberately separate from the AWS Terraform stack; must support WebSockets and pinning to exactly one instance
technology.localRegistry: Verdaccio (test-time only) for installing unpublished @swiftagent/* packages
technology.scaffoldCli: Node 22 + TypeScript, published unscoped as create-swift-agent
technology.license: Apache-2.0 (DECIDED 2026-08-19). Chosen over MIT for the explicit patent grant and patent-retaliation clause, which matter for infrastructure companies embed and deploy; it is also the norm among comparable projects. WS-44 replaces the current UNLICENSED fields and adds the repository LICENSE file.
technology.note: No changes to the runtime stack and no new runtime dependencies.

constraints.singleInstance: docs/runbooks/realtime-operations.md §1 and §6: connections, replay buffers, session locks, and in-flight runs are process-local; Redis pub/sub is wired but dormant; ECS is pinned to desired_count = 1. Every deployment surface this program creates must pin to exactly one instance with autoscaling disabled. Horizontal scale is Phase 2 and is out of scope. VERIFICATION: setting replicas or desired_count to 1 is necessary but not sufficient — SC-12 requires observing that exactly one instance serves traffic ACROSS a rolling deployment and a restart, since that is precisely when a managed host silently runs two.
constraints.forwardOnlyMigrations: docs/runbooks/migrations.md §1: migrations are forward-only via node packages/db/dist/migrate.js, with a drift preflight that refuses to apply on divergence. Deploy surfaces run migrate as an explicit release step; no down-migrations exist or will be added.
constraints.publishingSurfaces: DOMAIN (clarified 2026-08-19 round 2; closed over the TERMINAL repository 2026-08-20 round 4): the posture flip applies to the public packages and their public-consumer path ONLY. At program end the workspace holds FOUR public packages — @swiftagent/{sdk,react,shared} plus create-swift-agent, which WS-46 creates BORN public-postured (publishConfig.registry = registry.npmjs.org, access public, Apache-2.0, no private field) — and TEN private packages: @swiftagent/{api,db,gateway,models,observability,runtime,server}, the two quickstart example packages, and @swiftagent/playground, which WS-48 creates BORN "private": true. AGENTS.md's rule that every other package is private stays true after the flip. ORDERING: WS-44 sweeps every active surface existing at its time (the twelve below); packages created afterwards are born with the correct posture by their creating workstreams; and WS-49, the sole terminal workstream, re-runs the repository-wide active posture search over the terminal tree so exhaustiveness is checked against the repository that actually exists at program end. Within today's domain, going public means changing every ACTIVE surface that asserts or enforces the private/restricted posture, not the five originally listed. The complete active set: packages/{sdk,react,shared}/package.json (publishConfig + license); a repository LICENSE file; .changeset/config.json; docs/policies/versioning.md normative text; scripts/verify-pack.mjs assertions; .npmrc (which functionally routes @swiftagent:registry to npm.pkg.github.com and would otherwise keep sending consumer installs to GitHub Packages); the AGENTS.md Delivery convention at line 119; docs/as-built.md; README.md and docs/quickstart.md; packages/{sdk,react,shared}/README.md; .github/workflows/ci.yml and both publish-sdks workflows; and test/acceptance/install-published.ts, test/acceptance/install-registry.acceptance.test.ts, and test/vitest.acceptance.config.ts. Historical records — superseded program plans, task specifications, and as-built snapshots describing the posture that WAS true — are preserved as historical dispositions and are NOT rewritten; only active normative, functional, and shipped-documentation copies change.
constraints.contributionTerms: Apache-2.0 §5 licenses inbound contributions under the same outbound terms unless a contributor states otherwise, so a signed CLA is not required for the license to function. A DCO (Signed-off-by trailer, enforced in CI) is the proportionate instrument. Consequence to accept knowingly: contributors retain copyright in their contributions, so relicensing the project to different terms later would require their permission. A CLA would preserve that option at the cost of contributor friction; it is deliberately not adopted.
constraints.artifactAudience: Two distinct artifacts serve two distinct audiences: published npm packages serve the SDK consumer writing defineAgent/tool, while a published container image serves the runtime operator deploying the server. This program targets the operator, so the image is a first-class deliverable, not an optimisation. THE TWO ARE TRIGGERED DIFFERENTLY AND DELIBERATELY: npm publishing commits to a semver API surface and is effectively permanent once released, so the release workflow fires only from an explicit manual workflow_dispatch trigger — the actual release path per decision 4, pressed once by the owner; WS-44's checkpoint asserts the workflow property plus a dry run and completes without anyone pressing anything. The container image commits to no API surface, its references are replaceable, and it publishes automatically with no trigger — gated causally by WS-50 depending on WS-44 so the Apache-2.0 licence always lands before any image is published. No workstream in this program completes on a human approval step. GHCR BOOTSTRAP (corrected 2026-08-19, audit round 2): the compose pin is the sha256 MANIFEST-LIST DIGEST produced by the multi-arch push (image: ghcr.io/…@sha256:…). No tag satisfies "pinned" — version tags included — because GitHub's package lifecycle permits container package versions to be removed and replaced and GHCR defines no immutable-tag enforcement; only the content-addressed digest cannot drift. The digest cannot be referenced before it exists, so WS-50 publishes first and commits the compose digest pin as a second step within the same workstream. Version tags are published as human-readable aliases, never as the pin; upgrading means committing a new digest. Until the owner's one-time visibility click (decision 6), every in-program pull of the published image authenticates with documented registry credentials — the anonymous path is a post-click property the program documents but never asserts.
constraints.playgroundTakeaway: The playground exists to land one takeaway: "this is infrastructure, not a chat widget." It CANNOT demonstrate the product's central claim that tools run on infra the visitor controls — on a hosted demo they run on ours — so it must not imply otherwise. It proves what it can actually show, in this order: typed events you can build any UI on -> tool calls with real identity, timing, and failure semantics -> the session survives a dropped connection -> here is the code and the one command that reproduces it locally. Proving the tool boundary for real is the job of rungs 2/3 and of the proposed reverse-runner-transport program. BEATS 2 AND 3 CORRECTED 2026-08-19 after plan-audit: ChatEvent tool events carry callId, toolName, and status only (packages/shared/src/types/events.ts) — no deadline reaches the public surface, and ToolContext, ToolCallContext, RunnerRequestContext, and RunnerRequest omit it too. Beat 2 therefore renders a DEMO-OWNED timing budget: the playground configured that budget in its own tool wrapper, so it displays the configured value beside a duration measured from the real tool_call_started/tool_call_completed pair. No ChatEvent, runtime, or SDK surface is added. Beat 3 is corrected likewise: createChatSession().disconnect() sets intentionalClose and deliberately suppresses reconnection (packages/react/src/client.ts:211), so recovery is demonstrated by constructing a NEW session client against the same session id, and the on-page copy describes what actually happens rather than claiming an automatic reconnect.
constraints.canonicalGate: pnpm test (the configured verify gate) is FLAKY-RED at baseline as of 2026-08-19: apps/server/src/__tests__/index.test.ts awaits a dynamic import of ../index.js and takes ~2.5s of vitest's 5000ms default in isolation, so it intermittently times out under parallel turbo load. Observed failing on one full `pnpm test` run and passing on the next, with no source change between them. pnpm build, pnpm typecheck, and pnpm lint are green. Every workstream in this program must finish with all four commands green, so a gate that fails at random will fail checkpoints that are actually correct and trigger spurious replans. WS-51 makes the gate deterministic and is a hard dependency of both zero-dependency roots.
constraints.localBootstrap: SC-01 is NOT a two-value compose repair. A clean checkout has Postgres, Redis, and the listener and nothing else: test/smoke/realtime-smoke.ts requires a pre-seeded SMOKE_API_KEY and an existing smoke-echo agent, and does not self-provision. A `docker compose up` that completes a real tool round trip therefore additionally requires a server-accepted model configuration, a usable raw dev API key whose stored hash matches, a registered workspace and a tool-bearing agent, runner signing/verification keys with a reachable runner service, and a deterministic tool-calling model fixture. WS-43 owns all of it, which is why it is sized L rather than S.
constraints.npmGate: SUPERSEDED 2026-08-19 (audit round 3) by DECISION 4: the npm gate is REMOVED and publication is real. @swiftagent/{sdk,react,shared} AND create-swift-agent are released to public npm via a release workflow fired by an explicit manual workflow_dispatch trigger, pressed once by the owner when the program lands — that trigger is the release path, not an indefinite gate. The program delivers everything up to the button: public packaging metadata, the armed workflow (covering all four packages), a verified pnpm publish --dry-run, the local-registry end-to-end proof, and a release runbook documenting the trigger and the owner-owned npm org/token provisioning. Documentation is written for the released state (decision 4 authorizes this), with the runbook making the one remaining action visible; no surface asserts a version already exists on the registry. No workstream's checkpoint executes the publish or depends on the trigger being pressed.
constraints.ghcrVisibility: DECISION 5, 2026-08-19 (audit round 3, superseding the round-1 gh api decision, which rested on two false premises): GitHub exposes NO API operation to change package visibility — the REST packages API offers list, get, delete, restore, and version operations only — and packages do NOT inherit repository visibility (they inherit access permissions; newly published packages default to private). The repository wildorder/swift-agent was made public by the owner on 2026-08-19, which changes nothing about package visibility. The one supported mechanism is the manual UI step Package settings -> Danger Zone -> Change visibility -> Public, irreversible once public. The owner performs it ONCE after the first image publish (it is only possible once the package exists); WS-50 documents it as a repository-configuration prerequisite. DECISION 6, 2026-08-20 (audit round 4): autonomy wins — the program does NOT claim the click happened or that an anonymous pull succeeded. WS-50 ships a ready-to-run logged-out `docker pull` verification command the owner runs immediately after clicking, and every in-program consumer of the image before the click (the pulled-image equivalence check, CI compose pulls, the WS-47 deploy) AUTHENTICATES to GHCR with documented registry credentials, which become unnecessary once the package is public. WS-50's checkpoint asserts the workflow, publish, digest pin, documentation, and verification command — it does not block on, wait for, or assert the outcome of the owner's click.

successCriteria.description: From a clean checkout, `docker compose up` starts Postgres, Redis, and the server AND self-provisions everything a real turn needs — a server-accepted model configuration, a usable raw dev API key whose stored hash matches, a workspace and a tool-bearing agent, runner signing/verification keys with a reachable runner, and a deterministic tool-calling fixture — after which an automated smoke check completes a streaming turn over WebSocket asserting BOTH tool_call_started and tool_call_completed, with no manual seeding and no pre-supplied SMOKE_API_KEY.
docker-compose.yml contains no port or PUBLIC_WEBSOCKET_URL value that contradicts the single-listener behaviour in apps/server/src/main.ts.

@swiftagent/{sdk,react,shared} declare publishConfig.registry = https://registry.npmjs.org with access: public, carry "license": "Apache-2.0" backed by a repository LICENSE file (no UNLICENSED remains), and `node scripts/verify-pack.mjs` passes with assertions updated to match.

A `pnpm publish --dry-run` succeeds for all three packages — pnpm, not npm, because publication must go through pnpm to rewrite `workspace:*` dependency ranges to concrete versions, and the packed manifests are inspected to confirm that rewriting. The release workflow publishes to public npm ONLY from an explicit manual workflow_dispatch trigger — that trigger is the decided release path (decision 4), pressed once by the owner, and a release runbook documents it, including the owner-owned npm org/token provisioning. Demonstrated without the workstream itself publishing anything.

The local registry harness is a real npm registry protocol endpoint (Verdaccio) — a directory of tarballs or file: dependencies does not satisfy this — and it installs all three packages into a throwaway consumer that imports and type-checks against them, run as a repeatable command in CI.

create-swift-agent is packed and published INTO the WS-45 local registry (including its bin entry, verified from the packed tarball), and `npx create-swift-agent <name>` resolved against that registry produces a project that installs, type-checks, builds, and completes a streaming turn with a tool call — its generated-project test owning the same local runtime, API-key, and runner bootstrap that WS-43 defines. create-swift-agent is also included in the WS-44 release workflow, so the owner's single trigger releases it to public npm alongside the three packages (decision 4).

The deploy template provisions the runtime with managed Postgres and Redis on the chosen host, applies forward-only migrations as an explicit release step, and passes a health check, reproducibly from the documented button or command. Until the owner's GHCR visibility click, the host pulls the image using documented registry credentials, so this criterion does not depend on package visibility (decision 6); once the package is public those credentials become unnecessary and the docs say so.
The playground is reachable at a public URL and, in one session, streams tokens and surfaces at least one tool call in the event/trace panel with its start, completion, and duration.

Playground guardrails are enforced SERVER-SIDE by a trusted mediator that is the sole enforcement point between the browser and the playground's runtime — browser-side controls do not count as enforcement, the browser never receives the runtime workspace API key or any model-provider credential, the mediator holds the runtime API key, and the dedicated provider key is configured only as environment on the playground's isolated runtime deployment (the standard apps/server config path — no provider proxy and no runtime feature is added). Per-IP and per-session limits, a message cap, and a token cap are enforced in the mediator and tested against a client that ignores the UI; a global daily spend ledger persisted in Postgres, whose schema and migration WS-49 owns, survives restarts and settles atomically via reserve-then-settle against terminal RunRecord usage read from the public GET /v1/runs/:runId surface — settling against actual tokenUsage when the run completed with persisted usage, and settling CONSERVATIVELY AT THE FULL RESERVED ESTIMATE for any terminal run whose tokenUsage is null (failed, cancelled, and timed_out never persist usage; completed/failed/cancelled/timed_out is the exhaustive terminal family), never releasing a reservation below its reserved amount without persisted usage and requiring no runtime change; every refusal is delivered as a defined refusal frame of the mediator's own protocol — not a new ChatEvent variant, an unhandled error, or a dropped socket; and the deployed instance uses a dedicated provider key carrying a provider-side budget cap, documented with its configured value.

README.md links the live playground and the deploy button as working commands, and presents `npx create-swift-agent` and the `@swiftagent/*` package installs as the supported quickstart path for the released state (decision 4 authorizes writing documentation for that state, since release is the owner's single documented trigger away). A release runbook (or RELEASING section) documents exactly that trigger and the owner-owned npm org/token prerequisite, so the gap between merged docs and live packages is one visible, documented action — no surface invents a different install mechanism or claims a version already exists on the registry (no hardcoded version badges asserting a published version). docs/vision.md ladder statuses are consistent with that same released-state framing.

Evaluated over the TERMINAL repository at program end: for the four public packages — @swiftagent/{sdk,react,shared} and create-swift-agent — and their public-consumer path, no ACTIVE repository surface asserts or enforces a private/restricted publishing posture, and every other workspace package is "private": true — the nine current ones (@swiftagent/{api,db,gateway,models,observability,runtime,server} and the two quickstart example packages) plus @swiftagent/playground, which the program creates. The currently-existing in-domain surface set WS-44 sweeps is exhaustive and enumerated in constraints.publishingSurfaces: package metadata, LICENSE, .changeset/config.json, docs/policies/versioning.md, scripts/verify-pack.mjs, .npmrc, AGENTS.md, docs/as-built.md, README.md, docs/quickstart.md, all three package READMEs, ci.yml, both publish-sdks workflows, and the acceptance install harness plus its vitest config. Packages created after that sweep are born with the correct posture by their creating workstreams (create-swift-agent public-postured in WS-46, apps/playground private in WS-48), and WS-49 — the sole terminal workstream — re-runs the repository-wide active posture search over the terminal tree to close the claim against the repository that actually exists. Historical program plans, task specifications, and as-built snapshots are preserved unchanged as historical record.

Every deployment surface created by this program pins to exactly one running instance with autoscaling disabled, AND that is verified by observing a single serving instance across a rolling deployment and a restart rather than by configuration value alone; each ships documentation citing the single-instance rationale in docs/runbooks/realtime-operations.md §6.

A CONTRIBUTING.md and DCO file adopt the Developer Certificate of Origin 1.1 and state that contributors retain copyright; a CI check rejects a pull-request commit lacking a Signed-off-by trailer and accepts one that has it, asserted by the check actually running.

A multi-arch (linux/amd64 + linux/arm64) apps/server image builds and publishes to ghcr.io automatically from a workflow requiring no manual trigger, and a pulled image (pulled with documented registry credentials until the owner's visibility click; decision 6) starts, migrates, and serves REST + WebSocket identically to a locally built one.

docker-compose.yml consumes the published ghcr.io image pinned at its sha256 MANIFEST-LIST DIGEST (image: ghcr.io/…@sha256:…) — no tag satisfies this, version tags included, because GHCR permits container package versions to be removed and replaced and defines no immutable-tag enforcement — adopted only after that digest exists via the WS-50 staged bootstrap; the ONE-TIME owner UI step that makes the package publicly readable (Package settings -> Change visibility -> Public — GitHub exposes no API operation for this, packages default private regardless of repository visibility, and the step is only possible after the first push creates the package) is DOCUMENTED as a repository-configuration prerequisite together with a ready-to-run logged-out `docker pull` verification command the owner runs immediately after clicking — per decision 6 the program does NOT claim the click happened or that an anonymous pull succeeded, and no checkpoint waits on it; every in-program consumer of the image before the click (the pulled-image equivalence check, CI compose pulls, the WS-47 deploy) authenticates to GHCR with documented credentials; a clean-checkout run pulls rather than builds (authenticated in-program, credential-free for strangers once the owner has clicked, stated as exactly that); and a documented override still lets contributors build locally.

The playground delivers all four demo beats on the public surface with no runtime or SDK addition: raw ChatEvent JSON is viewable beside the rendered chat; a tool call shows callId, the demo-configured timing budget, and a duration measured from the real tool_call_started/tool_call_completed pair, and a deliberately failing tool can be triggered to show the failure path; a control drops the connection mid-stream and the session is recovered by constructing a new session client against the same session id, with on-page copy describing what actually happens; and the agent source plus the reproduce-locally command are shown on the page.

pnpm build, pnpm typecheck, pnpm lint, and pnpm test all pass deterministically from a clean checkout, with the apps/server index-export import-graph test no longer able to fail on a timing margin under parallel load; demonstrated by repeated cache-bypassed full-suite runs rather than a single green run, TWICE: once at WS-51 (the root repair) and again at the end of WS-49 (the sole terminal workstream), after apps/playground, packages/create-swift-agent, and every other workstream's packages and tests are in the tree.

scope.summary: Makes the four configured verification commands (pnpm build, typecheck, lint, test) pass deterministically, so every later workstream in this program can be judged on a gate that only goes red for real defects.
includes: Removing the timing margin in apps/server/src/__tests__/index.test.ts, whose dynamic import of ../index.js consumes ~2.5s of vitest's 5000ms default and times out under parallel turbo load

Auditing the other package test suites for the same shape — a bare `await import()` of a heavy module graph inside a default-timeout test — and applying the same fix wherever it is found, not only to the one observed failure
Establishing the fix as a convention (an explicit timeout, a hoisted static import, or a raised suite-level testTimeout) rather than an ad-hoc number, so new tests do not reintroduce the flake
Demonstrating stability by repeated full-suite runs with the turbo cache bypassed, not by one green run
excludes: Changing what any test asserts, or weakening an assertion to make it pass
Skipping, quarantining, or marking any test as expected-to-fail
Broad test-infrastructure work: no vitest workspace restructuring, no runner replacement, no parallelism/concurrency retuning beyond what removing the margin requires
Integration tests under the root test/ tree, which are excluded from the configured gate and run separately via pnpm test:integration under Testcontainers
Fixing product defects discovered while auditing; genuine server or SDK bugs are reported, not silently absorbed

The scaffold-generated compose file (owned by WS-46) and the managed-host deploy config (owned by WS-47), both of which consume this wiring rather than defining it

Packing create-swift-agent and PUBLISHING IT INTO the WS-45 local registry, with its bin entry verified from the packed tarball, so `npx create-swift-agent` is exercised through real npx resolution rather than a local file path
Project templates: an SDK backend with one Zod-schema tool, a Vite/React frontend using useAgentChat, a compose file matching the WS-43 wiring, and .env.example
Interactive prompts for project name and model provider/key, with non-interactive flags for CI

An end-to-end CI test that generates a project against the local registry, then installs, type-checks, builds, and completes a streaming turn with a tool call — the test owning the same local runtime, API-key, and runner bootstrap WS-43 defines, since a generated project has no seeded workspace either
Templates consuming only the public SDK surface, under the existing no-restricted-imports guard
Adding create-swift-agent to the WS-44 release workflow, so the owner's single manual trigger releases it to public npm alongside the three packages (decision 4)
excludes: Pressing the release trigger — create-swift-agent's real publication fires from the WS-44 workflow_dispatch pressed by the owner (decision 4); this workstream adds the package to that workflow and proves it end to end against the local registry
The program-wide documentation pass (README quickstart wording, vision ladder statuses, release runbook consistency) — that is SC-10, owned by WS-49
Deploy-target configuration for managed hosts (owned by WS-47)
The playground application (owned by WS-48) — the scaffold’s template is intentionally minimal, not the demo
Repairing the root docker-compose.yml or defining the local bootstrap (owned by WS-43); this consumes that wiring
A plugin system, multiple template variants, or framework choices beyond the single canonical template

scope.summary: Lets an adopter deploy the Swift Agent runtime into their own managed-host account from a button or a single command, on exactly one pinned instance with managed Postgres and Redis attached.
includes: A documented comparison of Fly.io vs Railway against fixed criteria (managed Postgres + Redis, WebSocket support, single-instance guarantee, idle cost, template format), with the decision recorded before implementation

Host configuration (fly.toml / railway.json or equivalent) deploying the published GHCR image from WS-50 rather than building from source on the host — pulling with documented registry credentials until the owner's one-time visibility click makes the package public (decision 6), so the deploy never depends on package visibility; the docs state the credentials become unnecessary post-click
Pinning to exactly one running instance with autoscaling disabled, documented with the rationale from docs/runbooks/realtime-operations.md §6
Provisioning and wiring managed Postgres and Redis, running forward-only migrations as an explicit release step per docs/runbooks/migrations.md, and passing a health check
Secret and environment documentation, including a correct public wss:// PUBLIC_WEBSOCKET_URL
A README deploy button and a self-host guide section
A reproducible verification that a fresh deploy comes up healthy

Verifying single-instance behaviour by observation rather than configuration: exactly one instance serves traffic across a rolling deployment and a restart, which is when a managed host is most likely to run two (SC-12)
excludes: Deploying the playground itself (owned by WS-49) — this delivers the reusable template, not the demo instance
Any change under infra/ or to the AWS dev/staging/prod Terraform stack and its workflows
Multi-instance, autoscaling, or multi-region configuration — process-local session state makes this incorrect until Phase 2
Custom domains or TLS termination beyond the host's defaults
Playground abuse controls and guest-session policy (owned by WS-49)

scope.summary: Builds the demo app around one stated takeaway — "infrastructure, not a chat widget" — delivered by four designed beats: a raw typed-event feed, a tool call with real identity and timing including its failure path, a survivable dropped connection, and the source plus the command that reproduces it locally.
includes: apps/playground/backend: an SDK agent with two to three genuinely useful tools whose calls are worth watching. The new @swiftagent/playground package.json is BORN "private": true — it joins the ten-package private roster of SC-11 and is never swept by WS-44, which precedes it

BEAT 1 — typed events, not text: the event panel renders the raw ChatEvent JSON (toggleable against the prettified view) so a visitor sees message_started -> token -> tool_call_started -> tool_call_completed -> message_completed and understands they can build any UX on it

BEAT 2 — a tool call is a real round trip: surface callId, the DEMO-OWNED timing budget, and the measured duration. The budget is the playground’s own: no deadline reaches the public surface (ChatEvent tool events carry callId, toolName, and status only), so the demo displays the budget it configured in its own tool wrapper beside a duration measured from the real tool_call_started/tool_call_completed pair. Include one tool that deliberately times out or errors, triggerable by a button, so the failure path is demonstrated rather than hidden — an infrastructure evaluator is asking "what happens when a tool hangs?", so answer it unprompted

BEAT 3 — survives a dropped connection: a control the visitor hits mid-stream that drops the connection, after which the session is recovered by constructing a NEW session client against the same session id. createChatSession().disconnect() sets intentionalClose and deliberately suppresses reconnection (packages/react/src/client.ts:211), so the demo must perform the recovery explicitly and the on-page copy must describe what actually happens rather than implying an automatic reconnect
BEAT 4 — the conversion beat: the ~20 lines of defineAgent/tool that produced the demo shown beside it, plus the one command that reproduces it locally

Building all four beats on the PUBLIC surface only, having verified datum by datum that each is reachable there. Where it is not — the tool deadline — the beat is satisfied from demo-owned state instead of by adding a surface
Guest session creation against a locally running runtime, with no signup
Consuming only the public SDK/react surface, enforced by the no-restricted-imports guard
Build, typecheck, lint, and tests green; exercised in CI like examples/quickstart
excludes: Claiming or implying that the visitor's tools run on their own infrastructure — on a hosted demo they run on ours; the copy must not overstate this, and proving it for real belongs to the proposed reverse-runner-transport program
Letting a visitor author, edit, or upload tool code — no server-side sandbox of any kind
Public deployment, the live URL, and anything requiring a hosting account (owned by WS-49)
Rate limiting, spend caps, and abuse controls (owned by WS-49) — this workstream runs locally and trusted
The deploy template itself (owned by WS-47)
New runtime, SDK, or react features. If a beat appears to need data the public surface does not expose, compose the public vanilla client or report the gap — do not add a hook or export
A marketing site, landing page, or docs site around the demo
Adding deadline (or any other field) to ChatEvent, ToolContext, or the runner protocol to make Beat 2 easier — explicitly rejected on 2026-08-19; the timing budget is demo-owned

scope.summary: Makes the playground safe to expose to the internet on the owner’s model budget — enforced server-side by a trusted mediator that is the sole enforcement point, with the provider credential confined to the playground runtime's own environment — deploys it publicly on a single pinned instance, proves the live URL works, owns the program-final documentation pass, and re-proves the verification gate at program end.
includes: A trusted server-side mediator between the browser and the playground's runtime that is the ONLY place limits are enforced. The mediator holds the runtime workspace API key; the browser holds no credential of any kind. The dedicated model-provider key is configured ONLY as environment on the playground's isolated runtime deployment — the standard apps/server config path (apps/server/src/config.ts validates it, apps/server/src/container.ts registers the providers) — so the mediator never touches provider traffic and no provider-proxy or runtime feature is added. Browser-side controls are presentation, never enforcement: a visitor can bypass anything the client decides
Per-IP and per-session rate limits, a per-session message cap, and a per-session token cap, enforced in the mediator and tested against a client that ignores the UI

A defined refusal frame every limit produces, delivered over the WebSocket as a typed, rendered message of the mediator's OWN app-level protocol — not a new ChatEvent variant, an unhandled error, a 500, or a silently dropped socket — with a test per limit

Atomic reserve-then-settle accounting: reserve an estimated cost before a run starts, settle when it ends against the terminal RunRecord usage read from the public GET /v1/runs/:runId surface, and release reservations for runs that never terminate, so concurrent sessions cannot race past the ceiling. SETTLEMENT RULE for the exhaustive terminal family: completed runs persist tokenUsage and settle against that actual usage; failed, cancelled, and timed_out runs never persist tokenUsage (packages/db/src/repositories/run-repo.ts fail/cancel/timeout write status only), so any terminal run with null usage settles CONSERVATIVELY AT THE FULL RESERVED ESTIMATE — a reservation is never released below its reserved amount without persisted usage, and no runtime change is made to persist usage on those paths

A global daily spend ledger persisted in Postgres, whose schema and forward-only migration THIS workstream owns and adds (it does not exist today). Not an in-memory counter — process-local state resets on every restart per docs/runbooks/realtime-operations.md §1, which would silently make the ceiling per-uptime-window rather than per-day
Short guest-session TTL and ephemeral retention configuration for the deployed instance
Deploying apps/playground to the WS-47 host target with its own database and secrets, isolated from dev/staging/prod, pinned to exactly one instance
A smoke test against the live public URL asserting a streaming turn with a visible tool call

A dedicated model-provider API key used only by the playground, with a provider-side budget cap configured on it — the backstop that holds even if the application limiter has a bug, is bypassed, or is misconfigured; documented as a required manual setup step with the cap value
A deliberately cheap default model for the playground, chosen to minimise blast radius before any limiter fires, with the choice and its cost rationale recorded
Alerting or a documented check at a fraction of the daily ceiling, so the owner learns about unusual spend from a notification rather than from an invoice

The SC-10 documentation pass: linking the live playground and deploy button as working commands, and presenting `npx create-swift-agent` and the @swiftagent/* installs as the supported quickstart path for the released state (decision 4), consistent with the WS-44 release runbook that documents the owner's single trigger — with no surface claiming a version already exists on the registry. This pass is why WS-49 depends on WS-46: the quickstart claim may only be published after the workstream that builds, verifies, and wires the scaffold into the release workflow has landed
Verifying single-instance behaviour by observation across a rolling deployment and a restart, not by configuration value alone (SC-12)

The program-final SC-17 gate re-proof: as the sole terminal workstream, finish with repeated cache-bypassed runs of pnpm build, typecheck, lint, and test, now that apps/playground, packages/create-swift-agent, and every other workstream's packages and tests are in the tree — complementing the WS-51 root repair, which proved stability before those packages existed

The program-final SC-11 posture sweep: re-run the repository-wide active private/restricted posture search over the TERMINAL tree — including the two packages created after WS-44's sweep — confirming the four public packages carry the public posture, the ten private packages carry "private": true, and no active surface contradicts either
excludes: Building the playground UI or its tools (owned by WS-48)
Authoring the deploy template (owned by WS-47) — this consumes it
Runtime-level retention modes (retention: none | metadata | full) — deliberately out of program scope; guardrails here are deployment configuration
Scaling the playground beyond one instance for load — the correct response to load is tighter caps, not more instances
Authentication, signup, or per-user accounts for the playground — it stays anonymous
Analytics, telemetry, or usage dashboards
Bring-your-own-key mode for visitors — a viable later fallback if spend proves uncomfortable, but out of scope here: the playground must stay a zero-friction 60-second demo

Claiming in any documentation surface that a version of any package already exists on the public registry before the owner fires the release — docs are written for the released state per decision 4, with the release runbook making the one remaining action visible (constraints.npmGate)
Enforcing any limit in the browser and counting it as enforcement

Owning or proxying the model-provider credential in the mediator — the credential lives only in the playground runtime's environment; routing provider traffic through the mediator would require a provider-proxy runtime feature or embedding the private server package, both forbidden (no runtime work, public surfaces only)

scope.summary: Builds and publishes the apps/server image to GHCR automatically as the operator-facing artifact, makes that package anonymously pullable, and repoints docker-compose.yml from building the monorepo from source to pulling it pinned at its sha256 manifest-list digest.
includes: A GitHub Actions workflow building apps/server/Dockerfile and publishing to ghcr.io automatically on the repository default branch and on release tags — no manual trigger and no human approval step; publishing is authorized, and depending on WS-44 guarantees the Apache-2.0 licence is already in the tree
Multi-arch builds (linux/amd64 + linux/arm64) so Apple Silicon operators are served

Documenting the ONE-TIME manual owner step that makes the GHCR package publicly readable: Package settings -> Danger Zone -> Change visibility -> Public, performed once after the first image publish (decision 5, constraints.ghcrVisibility). GitHub exposes NO API operation for this, and a newly published package defaults to PRIVATE — packages inherit repository access permissions, not visibility, so the repository being public (it is, as of 2026-08-19) does not make the package pullable. The step is irreversible once public and is documented as a repository-configuration prerequisite; per decision 6 the workstream's checkpoint does not block on, wait for, or assert the outcome of the owner performing it

Shipping a READY-TO-RUN verification command for anonymous reachability — a `docker pull` from a logged-out context, for the owner to run immediately after the visibility click — since a successful authenticated push does not demonstrate public distribution. The program delivers and documents the command; it does NOT run it as acceptance evidence or claim it succeeded (decision 6, SC-15)

Documented registry credentials for every in-program consumer that pulls the image before the click: the pulled-image equivalence check, CI compose pulls, and the WS-47 deploy all authenticate to GHCR; the docs state the credentials become unnecessary once the package is public

A tag strategy: version tags plus a moving tag as human-readable aliases, documented so operators know what they are pinning — with the explicit caveat that GHCR tags, version tags included, are mutable (package versions can be removed and replaced), so the only reference that cannot drift is the sha256 manifest-list digest produced by the multi-arch push

A STAGED BOOTSTRAP for the compose pin: publish first, then repoint docker-compose.yml from `build:` to `image: ghcr.io/…@sha256:…` at the manifest-list digest that now exists. The pin is the DIGEST, never a tag; it cannot be committed before its first publication; and the documented upgrade path is committing a new digest
A documented compose override (or profile) so contributors can still build from source
Build provenance/attestation where the platform provides it at no extra cost
Verifying a pulled image (pulled with the documented registry credentials until the click) starts, migrates, and serves REST + WebSocket exactly as the locally built one does
Operator documentation in README.md and the self-host guide: how to pull, pin, and upgrade
excludes: Gating the image push behind a manual trigger or human approval — deliberately authorized; the npm gate exists to protect a semver API commitment and does NOT transfer to a build artifact whose tags are replaceable

Treating GitHub REPOSITORY visibility as sufficient or necessary for package visibility — the repository is already public, but packages default private regardless; only the documented one-time package-settings UI step makes the package pullable (decision 5)
Attempting to change package visibility via gh api or any REST call — no such operation exists in GitHub's packages API; do not script what the platform only offers in the UI

Waiting on the owner's visibility click, running the anonymous-pull verification as acceptance evidence, or claiming anywhere that the anonymous pull succeeded — the click and its verification are the owner's post-program actions (decision 6)
Publishing any image other than apps/server (no playground, scaffold, or migration images)
Changing apps/server/Dockerfile’s build strategy or the --prod prune behaviour beyond what multi-arch requires
Signing infrastructure beyond what the platform offers for free (no cosign key management, no SBOM pipeline)
Repairing compose ports, PUBLIC_WEBSOCKET_URL, or the local bootstrap (owned by WS-43) — this consumes that corrected wiring
Any change under infra/ or to the ECR-based AWS deploy workflows, which continue unchanged

outOfScope: Pressing the npm release trigger inside any workstream — publication is real and decided (decision 4) but fires from the delivered workflow_dispatch pressed by the owner; provisioning the npm organization and token is likewise a manual owner-owned setup step, documented but not performed
Any change under infra/ (AWS Terraform stack, environments, deploy workflows)
Horizontal scaling in any form: shared session locks, shared replay buffers, cross-instance fanout, or autoscaling — Phase 2 per docs/runbooks/realtime-operations.md §6
Runtime retention modes (retention: none | metadata | full)
Any new runtime, SDK, or react feature: no new endpoints, SDK surface, model providers, or durable execution
A hosted multi-tenant service, billing, signup, or dashboard app
Removing GATEWAY_PORT or altering the standalone-gateway entry point

A docs site, code of conduct, or issue templates — CONTRIBUTING.md and the DCO are now in scope (WS-44) because contribution terms are part of the licensing posture; the rest of the community scaffolding is not
A CLA or copyright-assignment agreement — deliberately rejected; see constraints.contributionTerms
Publishing images for anything other than apps/server, and any container signing or SBOM pipeline beyond free platform-provided provenance

An AWS Bedrock model provider — no bedrock/* provider exists in packages/models today, and adding one is explicitly not part of this program; recorded as candidate future work in docs/vision.md. The playground uses direct provider keys, which give a stronger hard spend stop than AWS Budgets do.

Performing the one-time GHCR package-visibility change from inside a workstream, waiting on it, or asserting its outcome — it is a manual, irreversible owner UI action with no API equivalent, only possible after the first push (decisions 5 and 6); workstreams document it and ship the post-click verification command
Adding a tool deadline to ChatEvent, ToolContext, or the runner protocol. Rejected 2026-08-19 in favour of a demo-owned timing budget, preserving the no-runtime-feature-work rule.
